newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Fertiliser crisis to hurt Zambia 1997 maize yield.
newsitem.headline: Fertiliser crisis to hurt Zambia 1997 maize yield.

text.p: Zambia's maize yield is likely to drop in 1997 due to a fertiliser shortage caused by a government liquidity crisis last year, the agriculture ministry said on Thursday.

Agriculture permanent secretary Austin Sichinga said fertiliser imports were delayed because South African suppliers withheld supplies until the government had settled outstanding debts late last year.
"Our suppliers decided not to provide us with more supplies until we cleared arrears totalling $10 million for 30,000 tonnes of fertiliser they supplied in 1995," Sichinga said.
"We were supposed to have made the payments in March last year but only managed to do so in October," he added.

Western governments, led by the United States, froze funding to aid-reliant Zambia last year in protest against constitutional changes by President Frederick Chiluba aimed at giving his Movement for Multiparty Democracy advantage in a November 18 general election.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the polls, won by Chiluba in a landslide.
Sichinga said the government had now ordered 49,000 tonnes of fertiliser from South Africa at $26 million.
"The late arrival of the fertiliser is likely to have an adverse impact on the yield," he said.
Zambia requires a total of 225,000 tonnes of fertiliser a year for about 600,000 small-scale farmers and large commercial enterprises.
The government stock would provide for about 90,000 small-scale farmers, while the shortfall was expected to be met by private sector and donor supplies.
"The government cannot provide for all the farmers because it does not have the resources," Sichinga said.
Zambia produced 15 million 90-kg bags of maize last year, against a national requirement of 12 million.
While it was too early to predict the 1997 harvest the fertiliser shortage would probably mean it would be lower, Sichinga said.
